messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arthur is a 74-year-old widowed man who spent most of his adult life as a combat pilot, and he still carries himself with the controlled bearing of someone trained never to lose composure. The trauma he speaks of, however, happened not in combat but late in life, during a relationship that became physically abusive. His partner would approach him after drinking, the sharp smell of alcohol already enough to make his body tense, and arguments would turn quickly into grabbing, shoving, and striking. What stayed with him most vividly was the confusion of being touched in what should have been an intimate setting and suddenly realizing he was in danger. He remembers seeing her face at close range and feeling trapped by how quickly affection could become violence. Since the relationship ended, those sensory details have remained potent: the brush of an unexpected hand, the smell of liquor on someone’s breath, or even catching sight of her in town can make the past feel abruptly near.

In the months that followed, Arthur began organizing his life around not being caught off guard. If someone touched his shoulder unexpectedly, his whole body would jolt before he could think; if he passed a bar doorway and smelled alcohol, his chest tightened and his muscles braced as though he might need to defend himself. On the rare occasions he saw his former partner, even at a distance, he would immediately change direction or leave. Those moments pushed him toward a rigid set of rules that felt necessary to him: avoid anything connected to her, never let himself feel anger, and do not get emotionally close enough to anyone that he could be vulnerable again. He describes anger as especially dangerous. In his mind, if he allowed himself to feel it, it would either overwhelm his control or draw him back into the same kind of volatile closeness he had barely escaped.

Arthur’s sense of danger did not stay confined to obvious reminders. At night, he has difficulty falling asleep because he feels he needs to remain alert. He scans the house repeatedly, listens for sounds, and lies in bed with the kind of watchfulness that once served him in the cockpit but now leaves him exhausted. During the day he is similarly on guard, tracking who is nearby and where exits are. This constant readiness has only hardened his private rules. Because he is so watchful and keyed up, he doubles down on keeping people at a distance, avoids places where he might encounter his former partner, and clamps down even harder on any stirrings of anger. To Arthur, these choices feel like discipline rather than distress; he believes they are what keep him safe.

That same discipline has gradually narrowed his life. Although he still identifies strongly with his work as a pilot, the daily environment around aviation has become complicated for him. A congratulatory hand on the back from a colleague in the hangar can make him recoil internally, and if someone comes in carrying the faint smell of alcohol from the night before, he becomes physically tense and distracted. He has become adept at stepping away, rerouting conversations, and keeping interactions strictly professional. Over time, his avoidance of reminders has made those reminders seem even more charged. Because he works so hard never to see anything associated with his former partner, a chance sighting of her now feels almost unbearable. Because he avoids closeness, even benign touch has come to feel unfamiliar and threatening. The more he suppresses anger, the less he trusts himself when his body surges with it, and those surges are followed by even tighter self-control.

The cycle has deepened over the past year. His vigilance leaves him tired, and the fatigue makes him feel less defended, which in turn leads him to monitor his surroundings even more closely. When his body reacts strongly to a reminder—heart pounding, muscles tightening, a sudden startle—he takes that reaction as proof that the danger is still immediate, and he responds by withdrawing further from anything emotionally intimate or reminiscent of the relationship. Those efforts bring short-term relief, but they also keep his world small and his body ready for threat. He has not remarried since being widowed, and now he cannot imagine allowing anyone close enough to touch him casually or know him deeply. What finally brought him to treatment was the recognition that he is living as though the abuse is still about to happen: sleeping lightly, scanning constantly, and arranging his work and personal life around escape. He says he wants help because he is tired of feeling on guard in his own home, but what frightens him most is the possibility that lowering that guard, even a little, would leave him exposed again.
